slides.title: Raw Disks For Instances
slides.lead:
A block storage volume is a raw disk that an operating system partitions and formats itself
Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) is AWS's block storage service, giving each EC2 instance a persistent virtual disk

points.text: An EBS volume attaches to only one EC2 instance at a time
A volume lives in one Availability Zone and attaches only there
Volume data persists independently of the instance, surviving stop, start or termination
EBS volumes come in SSD-backed and HDD-backed families for different workloads

slides.notes: Explain that EBS gives an instance its own virtual disk, separate from its lifecycle. Note that the Availability Zone lock is a physical constraint, not a setting. Mention this will later contrast with shared file storage; interviewers often ask why EBS cannot attach across zones — the answer is physical replication boundaries.

slides.label: Analogy: an external hard disk
slides.title: Raw Disks For Instances
slides.notes: TR analogy: An external hard disk plugged into one laptop stores files only that laptop can read directly — just as an EBS volume attaches as a raw block device to a single EC2 instance at a time.

slides.title: Measuring Volume Performance
slides.lead:
Input/Output Operations Per Second (IOPS) counts individual read/write requests a volume completes per second, while throughput measures total data moved per second in megabytes
Together they describe volume speed from two angles
slides.notes: Explain IOPS and throughput as two separate speedometers. Contrast a database's many small writes with a video backup's one large sequential write, and note that optimising for the wrong metric is a common mistake. Interviews often ask which metric matters most for a given workload.

slides.title: Measuring Volume Performance

points.text: IOPS matters most for small, random reads and writes, such as transaction logs
Throughput matters most for large, sequential transfers, such as video streaming or backups
General purpose SSD volumes offer baseline IOPS and throughput that scale somewhat with volume size
Provisioned IOPS volumes let an application request guaranteed IOPS, independent of volume size

slides.notes: Explain IOPS and throughput as two separate speedometers. Contrast a database's many small writes with a video backup's one large sequential write, and note that optimising for the wrong metric is a common mistake. Interviews often ask which metric matters most for a given workload.

slides.title: SSD Versus HDD Backing
slides.lead: Different workloads need different performance profiles, so Amazon EBS offers volume types split into two backing media: solid-state drives for speed and hard-disk drives for lower-cost bulk transfer

cells: Boot volumes and most general workloads
Databases needing guaranteed, consistent low latency
Big sequential workloads like log processing
Infrequently accessed data at lowest cost

slides.notes: Walk through the table, noting the SSD-versus-HDD split first. Mention gp3 is the default choice for most workloads, while io2 trades cost for guaranteed performance. Interviewers may ask which volume type suits a workload — match the access pattern to SSD or HDD first.

slides.title: SSD Versus HDD Backing
slides.lead:
A database requiring 15,000 IOPS and 2,000 GiB of storage can use either gp3 or io2 without increasing storage capacity to achieve the required IOPS
gp3 offers a cost-effective option, while io2 suits mission-critical workloads requiring higher durability and consistently low latency
slides.notes: Walk through the table, noting the SSD-versus-HDD split first. Mention gp3 is the default choice for most workloads, while io2 trades cost for guaranteed performance. Interviewers may ask which volume type suits a workload — match the access pattern to SSD or HDD first.

slides.title: Where EBS Fits Best
slides.lead: Choosing a volume type means matching an application's access pattern to the right backing media, since the same workload on the wrong type either wastes money or starves for performance

points.text: Boot volumes store the OS and startup files, typically on general purpose SSD
Relational databases need consistent low-latency IOPS, favouring provisioned IOPS SSD
Big data and log-processing pipelines read large sequential files, favouring throughput-optimized HDD
Archival or rarely-touched data favours cold HDD for lowest cost

slides.notes: Map each use case to the volume type from the previous table. Contrast a database transaction with a nightly log dump, noting that EBS pricing scales with provisioned IOPS and throughput. Interview questions often ask which volume type fits a given workload.

slides.title: Where EBS Fits Best
slides.lead:
A nightly 500 GB log pipeline fits st1, priced per gigabyte with no per-IOPS charge
The same workload on io2's 15,000 IOPS would cost far more for unneeded throughput

chips.text: Far More Cost For Unneeded Throughput

slides.notes: Map each use case to the volume type from the previous table. Contrast a database transaction with a nightly log dump, noting that EBS pricing scales with provisioned IOPS and throughput. Interview questions often ask which volume type fits a given workload.

slides.title: Cost And AZ Limits
slides.lead: Block storage's performance comes with real constraints: a volume is locked to one Availability Zone and normally serves only one instance, so cost and location choices must be made upfront

points.text: Provisioned IOPS volumes cost more, so size workloads to actual need
A volume cannot attach across Availability Zones without a snapshot copy
Normally only one instance can mount a volume at a time
Over-provisioned IOPS or throughput sits idle, so right-sizing avoids paying for unused headroom

slides.notes: Stress that the Availability Zone lock is physical, not configurable; plan volume placement accordingly. Higher guaranteed IOPS cost more per gigabyte. Flag the single-attach limit as why shared file storage exists, without naming it yet; interviewers ask why an EBS volume cannot move between zones.

slides.title: Shared Filesystem Landscape
slides.lead:
File storage provides a shared filesystem that multiple servers mount like one common drive, instead of separate private disks
NFS and SMB carry this access

points.text: NFS originated on Unix and Linux, and remains the Linux standard
SMB (Server Message Block): originated on Windows, is the Windows file-share standard
Both protocols allow multiple clients to read and write the same files concurrently

slides.notes: Introduce file storage as the shared-drive model before naming NFS and SMB individually. Mention that AWS offers this as Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx, covered next. Exam hook: learners should recall that file storage means several machines mount the same filesystem at once.

slides.title: How NFS Works
slides.lead:
Network File System (NFS) lets a client mount a remote directory so it behaves as local, while data stays on the server
The client sends read, write and lock requests for the server to execute
slides.notes: Explain that mounting makes a remote folder look local to the application. Point out the stateless-versus-stateful split between NFSv3 and NFSv4 as a common interview question. Mention that Amazon EFS is built on the NFSv4.1 protocol.

slides.title: How NFS Works

points.text: NFSv3 is stateless, so each request carries full file-handle and offset information
NFSv4 is stateful, adding built-in locking, delegation, and improved security over TCP
Exports define which server directories are shared and their permissions
Concurrent writers to the same file need explicit locking to avoid corruption

slides.notes: Explain that mounting makes a remote folder look local to the application. Point out the stateless-versus-stateful split between NFSv3 and NFSv4 as a common interview question. Mention that Amazon EFS is built on the NFSv4.1 protocol.

slides.label: Analogy: an office notice board
slides.title: How NFS Works
slides.notes: TR analogy: An office notice board lets every employee read and pin updates on the very same board instead of each keeping a private copy — just as NFS lets every mounting client read and write the one shared copy of a file kept on the server.

slides.title: Windows File Sharing
slides.lead: Server Message Block (SMB) is the Windows protocol for sharing files, printers and named pipes over a network, exposing each shared folder as a network share

points.text: SMB authenticates each session against Windows user or domain credentials
Opportunistic locks: a client caches a file locally and gets notified of changes
SMB 3.0 added end-to-end encryption and multichannel transport for higher throughput
CIFS: the older, less efficient dialect that SMB replaced

slides.notes: Contrast SMB's session-based authentication with NFS's export-based permissions covered earlier. Note that Amazon FSx for Windows File Server offers SMB-based storage in AWS. Exam hook: ask which protocol pairs with which operating system family.

slides.title: Choosing File Storage
slides.lead: Block storage attaches to one instance at a time, so an application that needs several servers to read and write the same files needs a shared filesystem instead

points.text: Content management systems and shared home directories need concurrent multi-client access
Rendering or batch pipelines let many worker nodes share intermediate files
Amazon EFS scales automatically but costs more per gigabyte than object storage

slides.notes: Emphasise that the deciding question is whether more than one server must see the same files at once. Mention Amazon EFS's per-gigabyte pricing as the cost trade-off for that convenience. Exam hook: ask learners to justify choosing EFS over EBS for a specific shared workload.

slides.title: Buckets To Namespace
slides.lead:
Object storage keeps data as independent units, not files in folders or disk blocks, used for backups and media at scale
Amazon S3 is the AWS service used here

points.text: Bucket: top-level container holding objects, setting region, access and lifecycle rules
Object: one stored item, made of the actual data, a key and metadata
Key: the unique string that identifies an object inside its bucket

slides.notes: Open with the landscape before covering bucket, object, key, metadata and flat namespace. Name Amazon S3 as the AWS service so terms attach to a real product. Flag flat namespace as the structural point later slides revisit.

slides.title: Buckets To Namespace

points.text: Metadata: descriptive information attached to an object, kept separate from the data itself
Flat namespace: all objects sit at one level, no folder tree

slides.notes: Open with the landscape before covering bucket, object, key, metadata and flat namespace. Name Amazon S3 as the AWS service so terms attach to a real product. Flag flat namespace as the structural point later slides revisit.

slides.title: Data Key Metadata
slides.lead:
An object is the basic unit of object storage: data, a key and metadata bundled together
Unlike a disk file, an object keeps all three parts together wherever it is stored

points.text: Data: the actual bytes of the object, stored as an opaque blob
Key: a string that uniquely names the object inside its bucket
System metadata: content type, size and last-modified date, maintained automatically
User metadata: custom key-value pairs that an application attaches

slides.notes: Explain that every object bundles data, key and metadata together, unlike a plain disk file. Use the courier parcel analogy: package, tracking label, contents declaration. Note that system metadata is automatic while user metadata is custom, and ask which one a user can actually edit.

slides.label: Analogy: a courier parcel
slides.title: Data Key Metadata
slides.notes:
TR analogy (speaker notes): Use the courier parcel analogy: package, tracking label, contents declaration.

"Explain that every object bundles data, key and metadata together, unlike a plain disk file. Use the courier parcel analogy: package, tracking label, contents declaration. Note that system metadata is automatic while user metadata is custom, and ask which one a user can actually edit."

slides.title: Naming And Scope
slides.lead:
A bucket lives in one AWS region, and its name must be unique across all of AWS, since S3 uses it in every object's address
Objects inherit that region by default

points.text: Global uniqueness: no two AWS buckets can share the same name
Naming rules: lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, three to sixty-three characters long
Region pinning: a bucket stays in its chosen AWS region
Object count: a bucket can hold unlimited objects, with no folder limit

slides.notes: Stress that bucket names compete globally, unlike folder names that need uniqueness only within a parent. Mention that region choice affects latency and data location. A common exam trap is assuming bucket names are scoped to one account.

slides.title: Prefixes Simulate Trees
slides.lead:
A file system nests folders inside folders, but an object store keeps every object flat, addressed only by its key
Console tools fake folder views by splitting keys on a slash
slides.notes: Explain that S3 console folders are an illusion built from key prefixes, not real directories. Renaming a folder path is costly: every object sharing the prefix must be copied and rewritten. This design scales S3 to billions of objects; interviewers ask why renaming isn't instant.

slides.title: Prefixes Simulate Trees

cells: Single flat list of keys per bucket
Key string only; the slash is just a character
Operating system walks the directory tree
Client filters keys sharing one prefix
Means rewriting every key sharing that prefix

slides.notes: Explain that S3 console folders are an illusion built from key prefixes, not real directories. Renaming a folder path is costly: every object sharing the prefix must be copied and rewritten. This design scales S3 to billions of objects; interviewers ask why renaming isn't instant.

slides.title: Three Access Mechanisms
slides.lead:
Object storage exposes buckets and objects through a web interface, not a mounted drive
Three mechanisms govern access and control who can reach the data

points.text: REST API access: every read, write or delete runs as an HTTP request
Presigned URLs: a signed, time-limited link grants access without sharing permanent AWS credentials
Versioning: a bucket can keep every prior copy of an object under one key

slides.notes: Frame this as the mechanics behind the bucket-and-key model already taught: how something actually reaches an object. Mention that each of the three gets its own slide next. Interviewers often ask how S3 is accessed without a filesystem mount — this slide is the answer.

slides.title: HTTP Verbs And Auth
slides.lead:
Representational State Transfer (REST) access means every S3 operation is a plain HTTP request to the object's own URL
The console, CLI and SDKs are just wrappers around these same calls

points.text: GET retrieves an object; PUT uploads or overwrites it; DELETE removes it
Requests to private data are signed with AWS Signature Version 4, not passwords or cookies
The request URL includes the bucket name and object key as the resource path
An unsigned or wrongly signed request to private data is rejected with an HTTP 403 error

slides.notes: Say there is no drive letter, only a web address and a verb, and this is how every SDK call translates. Exam hook: ask what distinguishes GET from PUT on the same URL — the verb, not the address.

slides.label: Analogy: a bank locker
slides.title: HTTP Verbs And Auth
slides.notes: TR analogy: At a bank, you give the locker number and say what you want to do (open, put in, or close it), and the bank checks your ID before acting, just as a REST call names the object key and HTTP verb, and S3 checks the signature before acting.

slides.title: Temporary Signed Access
slides.lead:
A presigned URL is a signed link giving temporary access to a private object without sharing AWS credentials
Anyone with access to the object can generate it, and it works until it expires

points.text: The signature is computed from owner credentials, object key, and expiry timestamp
S3 checks the signature and expiry on each request and rejects expired links, with no app server involved
A browser or mobile app can upload or download directly, skipping the server
Validity windows typically run from minutes to several days, set at generation

slides.notes: Explain this as sharing a private file without making the bucket public. Mention the common use case of an app letting users upload directly to S3. Exam hook: ask who enforces the expiry — AWS, not the application — and why that matters for security.

slides.label: Analogy: a movie ticket QR code
slides.title: Temporary Signed Access
slides.notes: TR analogy: A movie ticket booked online gives you a QR code that lets you into one show at one time, without making you a theatre staff member. Once the show time passes, the QR code stops working, just as a presigned URL lets its holder reach one object for a limited time without ever receiving the owner’s AWS credentials.

slides.title: Keeping Prior Copies
slides.lead:
Versioning lets a bucket keep every prior copy of an object under the same key instead of overwriting it
Once enabled, each PUT creates a new version with its own version ID

points.text: A GET without a version ID returns the current version
Deleting an object adds a delete marker, not erasing earlier versions
Any version ID can be restored via explicit REST API request
Retaining every version raises storage cost, since each overwrite is billed separately

slides.notes: Tie this to the earlier point that a key is a flat name — versioning adds hidden depth behind it. Mention accidental-deletion recovery as the main reason teams enable it. Exam hook: ask what happens to storage cost if versioning stays on indefinitely.

slides.title: Performance Sharing Scale Cost
slides.lead: Block, file and object storage were each built around a different design goal, so picking one for a workload comes down to four questions rather than a single rule

points.text: Performance: how fast single operations complete, measured as IOPS, throughput or latency
Sharing: whether one instance or many clients can read and write the same data at once
Scale: how large the data can grow and how that growth is managed
Cost: whether billing follows provisioned capacity or actual consumption

slides.notes: Frame this as the exam-style question: given a workload, which storage type fits. State each dimension in plain words before the comparison table. Interviewers often ask how to choose between S3, EBS and EFS — this slide is the answer skeleton.

slides.title: Across Four Dimensions
slides.lead: S3, EBS and EFS differ across performance, sharing, scale and cost, along with how they are accessed and how long data lasts, so each suits a different kind of workload

cells: Block device formatted and mounted by the OS
Network file system mounted by clients

slides.notes: Walk the four highlighted rows first: performance, sharing, scale and cost, since these decide the choice. Then use the other rows for context. Interview hook: given a workload, ask learners to pick S3, EBS or EFS and justify it using these rows. A common trap is calling one type simply 'better' instead of the right fit for the workload.

slides.title: Across Four Dimensions

cells: Low-millisecond latency, throughput scales with use
Many clients via permissions, no shared filesystem
Normally one instance at a time, same Availability Zone
Fixed size, can be increased manually, not shrunk
Pay per GB used plus requests, lowest per GB
Pay for provisioned size, even if unused
Pay per GB used, higher per GB
Until deleted or removed by a lifecycle rule
Independent of the instance; root volumes deleted on termination by default
Independent of client instances until deleted
Boot disks and additional instance storage

slides.notes: Walk the four highlighted rows first: performance, sharing, scale and cost, since these decide the choice. Then use the other rows for context. Interview hook: given a workload, ask learners to pick S3, EBS or EFS and justify it using these rows. A common trap is calling one type simply 'better' instead of the right fit for the workload.

slides.title: Selection Criteria
slides.lead: Translating the table into a decision means matching the row that matters most for the workload to the storage type that wins on it

points.text: Amazon S3 suits objects accessed by key via console, CLI or API
Amazon EBS suits one instance needing disk-like storage in its Availability Zone
Amazon EFS suits multiple instances that read and write shared files
Selecting a service follows the application's access pattern, not habit or familiarity

slides.notes: Map each service to one example: EBS for a database's data files, EFS for a shared config directory, S3 for user-uploaded images. S3 stores objects, EBS gives block volumes, EFS gives a shared file system. Expect interview questions like 'design the storage layer for X'.

slides.title: Testing S3, EBS and EFS Storage on AWS
What Gets Tested
slides.lead: This practical builds one example of each storage type: an S3 bucket for objects, an EBS volume on one instance for block storage, and an EFS file system shared between two instances for file storage

steps.text: Store an object in S3 and confirm it downloads with the same content
Attach an EBS volume to one instance, format and mount it, then store a file on it
Create a shared EFS file system reachable from two separate instances
Write a file on one instance, read it from the other
Compare all three services on performance, sharing, scale and cost

slides.title: Verify Then Remove
slides.lead: When a file written on one instance is missing on the other, the mount listing on both instances usually reveals the cause

points.text: A disk-usage check confirms whether a shared file system is actually mounted there
A missing shared mount means the instance is still using its own local disk
A name-resolution check confirms the file system address is reachable before mounting

slides.label: Finished Lab
slides.lead: The finished lab leaves one S3 object, one file on the EBS volume of Instance 1, and one EFS file visible from both instances

props.title: Verify Then Remove
props.lead: Removing lab resources afterward follows a safe order so nothing shared or still in use is deleted by mistake

steps.text: Record the object name, volume ID and file system ID before removing anything
Unmount the EBS volume on Instance 1 and the EFS file system on both instances before detaching or deleting them
Delete only the extra EBS volume and file system created for this lab
Terminate only the two instances created for this lab, since termination cannot be undone
Empty and delete only the bucket created for this lab
Leave any shared networking from an earlier session untouched
